note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/11 Group 17/11.2 The chemical properties of the halogen elements and the hydrogen halides.md
outline: Halogens act as oxidising agents by gaining electrons; oxidising power falls from fluorine to iodine. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution. Halogens combine with hydrogen to give hydrogen halides, $\ce{H2 + X2 -> 2HX}$; reaction vigour generally falls down Group 17. The thermal stability of hydrogen halides decreases $\ce{HF > HCl > HBr > HI}$ because H–X bonds become longer and weaker down the group.

misconceptions.statement: Iodine displaces bromide because it is a halogen.
misconceptions.refutation: Oxidising power decreases down Group 17; iodine cannot oxidise bromide.
misconceptions.contrast: Chlorine displaces bromide and iodide, but iodine displaces neither.

misconceptions.statement: Only a displacement reaction can make the hexane layer purple.
misconceptions.refutation: Iodine already present dissolves in hexane even when no displacement occurs.
misconceptions.contrast: Count iodine added as well as iodine formed.

misconceptions.statement: Hydrogen reacts equally vigorously with every halogen.
misconceptions.refutation: Reactivity decreases down the group; fluorine combines explosively while iodine reacts slowly and reversibly on heating.
misconceptions.contrast: Compare fluorine and iodine with hydrogen.

misconceptions.statement: Hydrogen iodide is most thermally stable because iodine is largest.
misconceptions.refutation: The H–I bond is weakest, so HI decomposes most readily on heating.
misconceptions.contrast: HF has the strongest H–X bond and greatest thermal stability.

misconceptions.statement: Intermolecular forces determine the thermal stability of hydrogen halides.
misconceptions.refutation: Thermal decomposition depends on breaking intramolecular covalent H–X bonds; these weaken down the group.
misconceptions.contrast: Use intermolecular forces for boiling; use H–X covalent bond strengths for decomposition.
misconceptions.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c11.2.pdf pp.4–5; Cambridge 9701 s25 P13 Q19, bundle official key C.

worked.problem: Compare the thermal stabilities of hydrogen bromide and hydrogen iodide, explaining the difference using bond strengths.

steps.do: The H–Br covalent bond is stronger than the H–I covalent bond.
steps.why: The larger iodine atom forms a longer, weaker bond to hydrogen than bromine does.

steps.do: More energy is needed to break H–Br than H–I during decomposition on heating.
steps.why: Thermal stability depends on how readily the H–X bond can be broken.

steps.do: Therefore HBr is more thermally stable than HI; HI decomposes more readily on heating.
steps.why: The compound with the stronger H–X bond resists thermal decomposition more.

9701-11.2.1.motivate: Can chlorine turn colourless iodide solution brown while iodine cannot do the reverse? Displacement reveals which halogen accepts electrons more readily.
9701-11.2.1.establish: Halogen molecules act as oxidising agents by accepting electrons: $\ce{X2 + 2e- -> 2X-}$. Oxidising power decreases down Group 17, $\ce{F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2}$. A stronger halogen oxidises halide ions of any weaker halogen beneath it. For example, $\ce{Cl2(aq) + 2Br-(aq) -> 2Cl-(aq) + Br2(aq)}$; chlorine is reduced and bromide is oxidised. Bromine displaces iodide but cannot displace chloride. Iodine displaces neither chloride nor bromide. Iodine present in a mixture dissolves in hexane and makes its layer purple, whether iodine was added directly or produced by displacement.
9701-11.2.1.connect: The oxidising trend predicts both displacement and the general decrease in vigour of halogen reactions with hydrogen.
9701-11.2.1.note:
- Oxidising power: $\ce{F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2}$.
- A stronger halogen displaces a weaker halide.
- A purple hexane layer shows iodine is present.
9701-11.2.1.self_explain: Why does bromine displace iodide but fail to displace chloride?
9701-11.2.1.plain_words: Start with electron transfer: the halogen molecule accepts electrons and the halide ion loses them. Compare the two halogens before predicting a displacement. Separately ask whether iodine was already in the tube; purple hexane tells you iodine is present, not how it got there.

forms.example:
Predict what happens when bromine water is added to aqueous sodium iodide. Identify both electron changes.
1. Compare: bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine, so bromine can oxidise iodide.
2. Track electrons: $\ce{2I-(aq) -> I2(aq) + 2e-}$ and $\ce{Br2(aq) + 2e- -> 2Br-(aq)}$.
3. Add the half-equations: $\ce{Br2(aq) + 2I-(aq) -> 2Br-(aq) + I2(aq)}$. Both sides have charge minus two and two atoms of each element. Sodium ions are spectators.
4. Interpret: iodide loses electrons and is oxidised; bromine gains electrons and is reduced. If shaken with hexane, iodine gives a purple organic layer.
forms.check: X, Y and Z are chlorine, bromine and iodine in an unknown order. X2 oxidises Y- ions, and Z2 oxidises X- ions. Deduce the identities of X, Y and Z and their decreasing oxidising-power order. Write the balanced ionic equation for Z2 reacting with Y- and name the species oxidised and reduced. Consider two fresh tubes: tube A initially contains Z2 and excess Y-; tube B initially contains Y2 and Z- only. After mixing and shaking separately with hexane, predict the hexane colour in each tube and state whether its iodine was newly formed or present initially. No electron-transfer explanation is required for the colour answers.
forms.answer: X is bromine, Y is iodine and Z is chlorine. Oxidising power: Z2 > X2 > Y2 (Cl2 > Br2 > I2). Cl2 + 2I- -> 2Cl- + I2; iodide ions are oxidised and chlorine is reduced. Both hexane layers are purple/violet. Tube A contains newly formed iodine; tube B contains iodine that was present initially, since iodine cannot oxidise chloride.

9701-11.2.2.motivate: Hydrogen can form a hydrogen halide with every halogen, yet the conditions and reaction vigour differ greatly.
9701-11.2.2.establish: Halogens combine with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides: $\ce{H2(g) + X2(g) -> 2HX(g)}$. Fluorine reacts explosively even in darkness. Chlorine reacts slowly in the dark but rapidly or explosively in light. Bromine reacts on heating, less vigorously than chlorine. Iodine reacts slowly and reversibly on heating. Overall reactivity with hydrogen decreases down Group 17. This is consistent with the decreasing oxidising power of the halogens: their tendency to accept electrons falls down the group. State the relevant light or heat condition when comparing specific reactions.
9701-11.2.2.connect: The hydrogen halides formed here have H–X covalent bonds. Their varying strengths determine their thermal stabilities.
9701-11.2.2.note:
- $\ce{H2 + X2 -> 2HX}$.
- Reaction vigour generally falls from fluorine to iodine.
- Chlorine responds strongly to light; bromine and iodine need heating.
9701-11.2.2.self_explain: Why is iodine's reaction with hydrogen less vigorous than chlorine's?
9701-11.2.2.plain_words: All four halogens form hydrogen halides with hydrogen. Compare conditions as well as vigour: light is important for chlorine, heating is needed for bromine and iodine, and heated iodine gives a reversible reaction rather than complete conversion. Recall the previous card’s decreasing tendency to accept electrons down the group.

forms.name: Compare halogen reactions with hydrogen
wordings: Describe the conditions and relative vigour of two halogen reactions with hydrogen.
Compare hydrogen halide formation, including reversibility for iodine.
forms.example:
Compare hydrogen reacting with chlorine and with iodine.
1. Identify the common pattern: each forms a hydrogen halide, with two product molecules per hydrogen molecule.
2. Chlorine: $\ce{H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g)}$; sunlight can cause an explosive reaction.
3. Iodine: heat the mixture; $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$. Reaction is slow and reversible, giving an equilibrium mixture in a closed system rather than complete conversion.
4. Link the comparison: iodine is below chlorine in the group and is the weaker oxidising agent. This is consistent with the lower reaction vigour; do not treat the required conditions as identical.
forms.check: Two particle models each start with five H2 molecules and three X2 molecules, with no hydrogen halide initially. In model A, X is bromine and the limiting reactant is assumed to react completely. In model B, X is iodine and a closed heated mixture reaches equilibrium containing four HI molecules. For each model, give the final numbers of hydrogen halide, H2 and X2 molecules, showing your particle accounting. A student claims that model B stopped changing because all of one reactant was used up. Use your counts to assess this claim and explain what the unchanged equilibrium composition means for the forward and reverse reactions.
forms.answer: A: six HBr molecules, two H2 molecules and zero Br2 molecules; three H2 and three Br2 make six HBr. B: four HI molecules, three H2 molecules and one I2 molecule; making four HI uses two H2 and two I2. The claim is false because both reactants remain in B. At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so composition has no net change.

9701-11.2.3.motivate: Why does heating hydrogen iodide produce iodine more readily than heating hydrogen bromide? Compare the bonds that must break.
9701-11.2.3.establish: Thermal stability means resistance to decomposition on heating. Hydrogen halide thermal stability decreases $\ce{HF > HCl > HBr > HI}$. Down Group 17 the halogen atom grows larger; the H–X covalent bond length increases and its strength decreases. Less energy is needed to break the weaker bond, so decomposition becomes easier. The H–F bond is strongest and HF is most thermally stable. The H–I bond is weakest and HI is least thermally stable. Compare intramolecular H–X bond strengths, rather than intermolecular forces, when explaining this trend.
9701-11.2.3.connect: The iodine produced on heating HI reflects the low thermal stability of HI; it does not reverse the oxidising-power order of halogens.
9701-11.2.3.note:
- Thermal stability is resistance to decomposition on heating.
- Stability: $\ce{HF > HCl > HBr > HI}$.
- H–X bonds become longer and weaker down the group.
9701-11.2.3.self_explain: Which bond is stronger, H–Br or H–I, and what does that predict on heating?
9701-11.2.3.plain_words: Heating can break the covalent bond joining hydrogen to the halogen. A larger halogen atom makes a longer, weaker H–X bond. Less energy is then needed to break it, so the compound decomposes more readily. Start from the bond inside the molecule, rather than forces between molecules.

forms.name: Explain a thermal-stability comparison using H–X bonds
wordings: Compare the thermal stabilities of two hydrogen halides.
Explain the trend using atomic size, bond length and covalent bond strength.
forms.example:
Explain why HCl is more thermally stable than HI.
1. Compare atoms: iodine is larger than chlorine.
2. Compare bonds: H–I is longer and weaker than H–Cl.
3. Connect energy: less energy is needed to break the H–I covalent bond, so HI decomposes more readily on heating.
4. Conclude: HCl is more thermally stable. This explains chemical decomposition; a boiling-point comparison would instead involve intermolecular forces.
forms.check: U and V are hypothetical halogens that follow the Group 17 hydrogen-halide trends; U has the larger atomic radius. A student records the following covalent bond energies: H–U, 430 kJ mol^-1; H–V, 300 kJ mol^-1. The two energy labels have been interchanged. Correct the assignments, predict which hydrogen halide is more thermally stable, and explain using relative bond length, strength and energy needed for bond breaking. State whether the relevant bonds are within or between molecules.
forms.answer: H–U should be 300 kJ mol^-1 and H–V should be 430 kJ mol^-1. Since U is larger, H–U is longer and weaker than H–V. More energy is needed to break H–V, so HV resists decomposition more strongly and is more thermally stable than HU. These are covalent bonds within molecules, not intermolecular forces.
